cards.title: MRSA and Zika Virus Infections
cards.content:
This lesson covers two short but frequently tested Chapter 1 guidelines.

**Section I.C.1.e: MRSA conditions.** **MRSA** stands for **methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus**, a bacterium that does not respond to the antibiotic methicillin. The guideline tells you:
• When to use a **combination code** (one code that names both the condition and the organism)
• When to use a condition code **plus B95.62**
• How to code **colonization** (carrying the organism without illness) for both MRSA and **MSSA** (methicillin susceptible Staphylococcus aureus)

**Section I.C.1.f: Zika virus infections.** This guideline is about **uncertain diagnoses**: Zika is coded only when **confirmed**, which is an exception to the usual inpatient rule for uncertain diagnoses.

boxes.b: Combination code vs B95.62; colonization Z22.32-

cards.title: In Plain English: MRSA Combination Codes (I.C.1.e.1.a)
cards.content:
A **combination code** is a single code that captures two things at once, here **the condition** and **the organism (MRSA)**.

**Rule:** If the patient's infection is due to MRSA and that infection **has a combination code** that includes the organism, assign the combination code. The guideline's examples:
• **A41.02**, Sepsis due to Methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus
• **J15.212**, Pneumonia due to Methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus

**Do NOT add:**
• **B95.62**, Methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus infection as the cause of diseases classified elsewhere, because the combination code already includes both the infection type and the MRSA organism
• A code from subcategory **Z16.11**, Resistance to penicillins

For MRSA sepsis, the sepsis rules in Section I.C.1.d still apply to sequencing (the guideline cross-references them).

boxes.b: The combination code, e.g. A41.02 or J15.212
B95.62 - organism already in the code
Code from Z16.11, Resistance to penicillins

cards.question: A patient is diagnosed with pneumonia due to MRSA. According to Section I.C.1.e.1.a, how should this be coded?
options: J15.212 only, with no B95.62 and no Z16.11 code
A pneumonia code plus B95.62
J15.212 plus a code from subcategory Z16.11
cards.explanation: Correct: Section I.C.1.e.1.a says that when an MRSA infection has a combination code, assign it (e.g., J15.212, Pneumonia due to Methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus), and do not assign B95.62 or a code from subcategory Z16.11. Option A is wrong because B95.62 is redundant with the combination code. Option C is the method for infections that have no combination code (I.C.1.e.1.b). Option D is wrong because Z16.11 is specifically not assigned.

visual.hint: Does a single code already name both the condition and the organism?

cards.title: In Plain English: No Combination Code (I.C.1.e.1.b)
cards.content:
Some infections do **not** have a combination code that includes MRSA. The guideline gives examples of current infections such as a **wound infection**, a **stitch abscess**, and a **urinary tract infection**.

**Rule:** When there is documentation of a **current** infection due to MRSA and no combination code exists:
1. Assign the code for the **condition** (the infection)
2. Add **B95.62**, Methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus infection as the cause of diseases classified elsewhere
3. Do **not** assign a code from subcategory **Z16.11**, Resistance to penicillins

**Exam trap:** The Z16.11 rule is the same in both situations (1.a and 1.b): it is not assigned for MRSA infections. What changes is only whether B95.62 is needed.

cards.title: Example: MRSA Wound Infection vs MRSA Sepsis
cards.content:
**Scenario A:** The provider documents a current stitch abscess due to MRSA.
• A stitch abscess is one of the current-infection examples listed in I.C.1.e.1.b; here, assume no combination code includes MRSA.
• **Section I.C.1.e.1.b:** code the stitch abscess **plus B95.62**. No Z16.11 code.

**Scenario B:** The provider documents sepsis due to MRSA.
• Sepsis has a combination code: **A41.02**, Sepsis due to Methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus.
• **Section I.C.1.e.1.a:** assign A41.02. Do **not** add B95.62 or Z16.11.
• Follow Section I.C.1.d for sepsis sequencing (and add R65.2 only if severe sepsis or associated organ dysfunction is documented).

cards.question: The provider documents a urinary tract infection due to MRSA. This infection has no combination code that includes the organism. Per Section I.C.1.e.1.b, what is assigned?
options: The urinary tract infection code plus B95.62
Only the urinary tract infection code
The urinary tract infection code plus Z16.11
B95.62 only
cards.explanation: Correct: Section I.C.1.e.1.b says that for a current MRSA infection without a combination code, assign the code for the condition along with B95.62, and do not assign a code from subcategory Z16.11. Option B leaves out the organism. Option C is wrong because Z16.11 is specifically not assigned. Option D is wrong because B95.62 identifies the organism causing a disease classified elsewhere, so the condition itself must also be coded.

visual.hint: What identifies the organism when the condition code does not?

cards.title: In Plain English: Colonization (I.C.1.e.1.c)
cards.content:
**Colonization** (also called **carriage**) means MSSA or MRSA is **present on or in the body without necessarily causing illness**. A person who is colonized is called a **carrier**.

The provider might document a positive colonization test as **"MRSA screen positive"** or **"MRSA nasal swab positive."**

**Codes:**
• MRSA colonization: **Z22.322**, Carrier or suspected carrier of Methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus
• MSSA colonization: **Z22.321**, Carrier or suspected carrier of Methicillin susceptible Staphylococcus aureus

**What it does NOT mean:** Colonization is **not necessarily** a disease process or the cause of a condition the patient has, **unless the provider documents it as such**. A positive screen is not an infection by itself.

boxes.b: Only if the provider documents it

cards.title: In Plain English: Colonization AND Infection (I.C.1.e.1.d)
cards.content:
Sometimes a patient is documented as having **both** MRSA colonization **and** an MRSA infection during the same hospital admission.

**Rule:** Both may be assigned:
• **Z22.322**, Carrier or suspected carrier of Methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus
• A code for the **MRSA infection** (a combination code, or the condition code plus B95.62, following 1.a and 1.b)

**Exam trap:** Students sometimes think the infection code "absorbs" the carrier status. The guideline says the two **may both be assigned** when both are documented.

visual.title: Both Documented
visual.sub: Section I.C.1.e.1.d: both may be assigned

cards.question: A patient's chart shows "MRSA nasal swab positive." The provider documents MRSA colonization and no infection. According to Section I.C.1.e.1.c, which code is assigned?
cards.explanation: Correct: Section I.C.1.e.1.c says to assign Z22.322, Carrier or suspected carrier of Methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus, for patients documented as having MRSA colonization, and notes a positive colonization test may be documented as "MRSA nasal swab positive." Option A is for a current MRSA infection without a combination code. Option B is for MSSA colonization. Option C is MRSA sepsis, which is not documented.

visual.hint: Colonization is not the same as infection.

cards.question: During one admission, the provider documents both MRSA colonization and an MRSA infection. Per Section I.C.1.e.1.d, what is correct?
options: Code only the infection
Code only Z22.322
Z22.322 and a code for the MRSA infection may both be assigned
Query the provider, because both cannot exist at once
cards.explanation: Correct: Section I.C.1.e.1.d states that if a patient is documented as having both MRSA colonization and infection during a hospital admission, Z22.322 and a code for the MRSA infection may both be assigned. Options A and B each drop a documented condition. Option D is wrong because the guideline expressly addresses this combination, so no query is needed on that basis.

visual.hint: Can both be reported in the same admission?

cards.title: In Plain English: Zika Virus (I.C.1.f.1)
cards.content:
**Rule:** Code only a **confirmed** diagnosis of Zika virus, as documented by the provider: **A92.5, Zika virus disease**.

**What counts as confirmed?** The provider's **diagnostic statement that the condition is confirmed** is enough. The documentation does **not** need to state the type of test performed.

**Mode of transmission:** A92.5 is assigned **regardless of the stated mode of transmission**.

**Not confirmed:** If the provider documents **"suspected," "possible," or "probable"** Zika, do **not** assign A92.5. Instead assign:
• Code(s) for the **reason for the encounter** (such as fever, rash, or joint pain), or
• **Z20.821**, Contact with and (suspected) exposure to Zika virus

boxes.b: Symptoms (fever, rash, joint pain) or Z20.821

cards.title: Exam Trap: Zika vs the Inpatient Uncertain Diagnosis Rule
cards.content:
**Section II.H (Uncertain Diagnosis)** normally says that for **inpatient** admissions, if the diagnosis at discharge is qualified as "probable," "suspected," "possible," and similar terms, you code the condition **as if it existed**. (Section II.H applies only to inpatient admissions to short-term, acute, long-term care and psychiatric hospitals.)

**Section I.C.1.f.1 says Zika is an exception to Section II.H.** Even for an inpatient, "suspected Zika" or "probable Zika" is **not** coded as A92.5.

**Bottom line:**
• Most inpatient uncertain diagnoses: code as if established (II.H)
• Zika: code only if confirmed by the provider (I.C.1.f.1)

visual.title: Uncertain Diagnosis Rules

boxes.b: Probable/suspected: code as if it existed

visual.sub: Section I.C.1.f.1 is an exception to Section II.H

cards.question: An inpatient's discharge summary states "probable Zika virus disease" with fever and rash. According to Section I.C.1.f.1, how should this be coded?
options: A92.5, because inpatient uncertain diagnoses are coded as if they existed
Codes for the fever and rash, or Z20.821, but not A92.5
Query the provider for the type of test performed before assigning A92.5
cards.explanation: Correct: Section I.C.1.f.1 says if the provider documents "suspected," "possible" or "probable" Zika, do not assign A92.5; assign code(s) explaining the reason for the encounter (such as fever, rash, or joint pain) or Z20.821. Option A is wrong because this guideline is an exception to inpatient guideline Section II.H. Option C is wrong because A92.5 is not assigned for probable Zika. Option D is wrong because confirmation does not require documentation of the type of test; the issue here is that Zika is only probable.

visual.hint: This guideline is an exception to the inpatient uncertain diagnosis rule.

cards.question: The provider documents "Zika virus disease, confirmed" but does not state which test was performed. The patient acquired the infection through a route other than a mosquito bite. Per Section I.C.1.f.1, what is assigned?
options: A92.5, Zika virus disease
Z20.821, because the test type is not documented
Nothing until the test type and mode of transmission are documented
Symptom codes only
cards.explanation: Correct: Section I.C.1.f.1 says confirmation does not require documentation of the type of test performed; the provider's diagnostic statement that the condition is confirmed is sufficient, and A92.5 is assigned regardless of the stated mode of transmission. Option B is wrong because Z20.821 is for suspected cases or exposure. Option C is wrong because neither the test type nor the transmission mode is required. Option D is wrong because the diagnosis is confirmed, so A92.5 is assigned.

visual.hint: What does the guideline say is sufficient for confirmation?

cards.title: Applying I.C.1.e and I.C.1.f on a Real Record
cards.content:
**MRSA documentation:**
1. Is it an **infection** or **colonization**? "MRSA screen positive" or "nasal swab positive" points to colonization; infection must be documented by the provider (I.C.1.e.1.c).
2. **Colonization only:** Z22.322 (MRSA) or Z22.321 (MSSA).
3. **Infection:** does the condition have a **combination code** with MRSA (e.g., A41.02, J15.212)? If yes, use it alone (I.C.1.e.1.a). If no, code the condition plus **B95.62** (I.C.1.e.1.b).
4. Never add a **Z16.11** code for MRSA infections.
5. **Both** colonization and infection documented? Both may be coded (I.C.1.e.1.d).
6. MRSA sepsis? Also apply Section I.C.1.d.

**Zika documentation:**
1. Is the diagnosis **confirmed** by the provider? Then **A92.5**, no matter the test type or transmission mode.
2. Suspected, possible, or probable? Code the **symptoms** or **Z20.821**. This applies in the inpatient setting too.

boxes.b: Combination code? If not, add B95.62

cards.title: Key Takeaways
cards.content:
• MRSA infection **with a combination code** (e.g., A41.02, J15.212): assign the combination code only, no B95.62 (I.C.1.e.1.a).
• MRSA infection **without a combination code** (e.g., wound infection, stitch abscess, UTI): condition code **plus B95.62** (I.C.1.e.1.b).
• **Never** add a Z16.11 code, Resistance to penicillins, for an MRSA infection (I.C.1.e.1.a-b).
• **Colonization** = present without necessarily causing illness: **Z22.322** (MRSA), **Z22.321** (MSSA). Not a disease unless the provider says so (I.C.1.e.1.c).
• Colonization and infection documented together: **both may be coded** (I.C.1.e.1.d).
• Zika: code **A92.5** only when **confirmed** by the provider; test type and mode of transmission are not required (I.C.1.f.1).
• Suspected, possible, or probable Zika: **symptoms** or **Z20.821**. This is an **exception to Section II.H**.

cards.question: Which situation calls for code Z22.321?
options: A patient documented as having MRSA colonization
A patient with a stitch abscess due to MRSA
A patient with suspected Zika exposure
A patient documented as having MSSA colonization
cards.explanation: Correct: Section I.C.1.e.1.c says to assign Z22.321, Carrier or suspected carrier of Methicillin susceptible Staphylococcus aureus, for patients documented as having MSSA colonization. Option A takes Z22.322. Option B is coded with the condition code plus B95.62 (I.C.1.e.1.b). Option C relates to Z20.821 (I.C.1.f.1).

visual.hint: Susceptible vs resistant: which one is MSSA?

cards.question: A provider documents "MRSA screen positive" and, separately, a cellulitis that the provider does not attribute to MRSA. Under Section I.C.1.e.1.c, how should the coder treat the colonization?
options: Assume the cellulitis is caused by MRSA and add B95.62
Do not report colonization when any infection is present
Report the colonization as Z22.322; colonization is not necessarily the cause of a condition unless the provider documents it
Report Z16.11 to show resistance
cards.explanation: Correct: Section I.C.1.e.1.c says colonization is not necessarily indicative of a disease process or the cause of a specific condition the patient may have unless documented as such by the provider; MRSA colonization is reported with Z22.322. Option A is wrong because the coder may not assume the link. Option B is wrong because nothing in the guideline drops colonization when an infection is present (I.C.1.e.1.d even allows both for MRSA infection). Option D is wrong because Z16.11 is not assigned in the MRSA guideline's instructions.

visual.hint: Who decides whether the colonization caused the condition?
